title: Supply-chain security in CI/CD
description: Secure every stage of the CI/CD pipeline from source code to deployed artifact against tampering and dependency attacks.

data.text: Software supply chain attacks exploit the trust between your code, your dependencies, and your build tools. If an attacker can inject malicious code into a package you consume, or alter your build output before it reaches production, they can compromise your entire application without ever touching your source repository.

Securing the supply chain in CI/CD means verifying who wrote the code, validating every dependency, measuring reproducibility, and proving that the artifact running in production is the same one your pipeline built.

data.title: Common attack vectors
items: Dependency confusion: attacker publishes a package with the same name as an internal package to a public registry.
Compromised maintainer: attacker takes over a legitimate package and injects malicious code.
CI token theft: attacker steals a pipeline token and pushes a malicious artifact.
Build tampering: attacker modifies build scripts or runners to inject code during compilation.

data.text: Lock files such as package-lock.json, packages.lock.json, or Pipfile.lock pin exact dependency versions. They are your first defense against dependency confusion. Always commit lock files to source control and never allow pipelines to resolve dependencies from mutable registries without validation.

data.title: Validate dependencies in CI
data.content: Fail the build if the lock file is missing, out of date, or contains known vulnerabilities.
data.code:
jobs:
  dependency-check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
        with:
          dotnet-version: "8.0.x"
      - run: dotnet restore --locked-mode
      - uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
        with:
          sarif_file: results.sarif

data.text: Signing an artifact means attaching a cryptographic signature that proves it was built by your pipeline and has not been modified. Sigstore, Azure Sign Tool, and Docker Content Trust are common signing mechanisms. When you combine signing with a software bill of materials, or SBOM, you get a verifiable record of exactly what went into each release.

terms.definition: Software Bill of Materials. A list of every component, dependency, and version included in an artifact.
Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts. A security framework that defines provenance and build integrity standards.
A free, open-source project that simplifies signing and verifying software artifacts.

data.title: Use SLSA for build integrity
data.text: SLSA defines how to make your build process verifiable. Start with SLSA Level 1 by generating provenance metadata, then progress to Level 3 by hardening your build service and verifying source and build integrity.

Your pipeline is itself a high-value target. Limit who can modify workflow files, require pull request reviews for workflow changes, and use OIDC to avoid long-lived secrets. In GitHub Actions, use the permissions key to restrict workflow tokens to the minimum required access.

data.title: Least-privilege GitHub Actions workflow
data.content: The workflow explicitly limits token permissions to read-only for most operations.
data.code:
name: Secure Pipeline
on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]
permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write
  id-token: write
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: sigstore/gh-action-sigstore-artifacts@v2
        with:
          inputs: out/
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: signed-app
          path: out/*.sig

items.text: Lock files are committed and restored with locked mode in CI.
items.hint: Block builds that modify lock files unexpectedly.

items.text: Dependencies are scanned for known vulnerabilities in every build.
items.hint: Use GitHub Dependabot, Snyk, or Grype.

items.text: Artifacts are signed before they leave the pipeline.
Workflow changes require pull request review.
Long-lived secrets are replaced with OIDC or short-lived tokens.
items.hint: Rotate any secret older than 90 days.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Supply chain attacks target dependencies and build pipelines, not just application code.
Lock files, dependency scanning, and artifact signing form a layered defense.
SLSA and SBOMs provide verifiable evidence of what you built and how.
Harden your CI/CD platform itself; it is a high-value target.
data.takeaway: Security is only as strong as the weakest link in the chain from commit to production.

items.question: Is signing really necessary for internal applications?
items.answer: Yes. Internal applications still run on production infrastructure. An attacker who compromises an internal dependency or build tool can pivot to production systems. Signing makes tampering detectable.

items.question: What is the fastest way to improve supply chain security?
items.answer: Enable Dependabot or an equivalent dependency scanner, require pull request reviews for workflow changes, and enforce locked dependency restores in CI. These three steps block the most common attack vectors.
